title: Serving LLMs at Scale: The Hidden KV Cache Advantage
gist: Momento CEO Khawaja Shams (ex-AWS DynamoDB) argues GPU scarcity makes LLM inference a distributed-systems utilization problem centred on KV cache memory: his experiments on a 4B model show p99 time-to-first-token jumping from 2.6s to 38.9s when concurrent sessions exceed GPU memory, with DRAM tiering, cache-aware routing, and prefill/decode disaggregation as the converging fixes. He predicts inference stacks will commoditize like databases did.

insights.claim: GPUs are among the scarcest resources and data centers are also constrained, so improving GPU utilization in the inference stack directly translates into better availability, performance, and economics.
insights.so_what: Software that raises inference utilization (caching, routing) captures value from the GPU shortage.
insights.quote: If you have better utilization, if you can use the capacity better, then that leads to better availability, it leads to better performance, and it leads to better economics.
insights.locator: Perspective of a Distributed Systems Engineer
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Classic distributed-systems problems such as routing, tail latency, and caching reappear inside LLM inference stacks, creating a 'renaissance' opportunity for systems engineers rather than ML specialists.
insights.so_what: Infra/data companies without ML pedigree can credibly compete in inference optimization.
insights.quote: this is going to be a renaissance for us distributed systems people
insights.locator: Perspective of a Distributed Systems Engineer
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Running your own inference stack will become commoditized and common within a couple of years, analogous to how expensive proprietary database racks of the 1990s gave way to simply turning on Postgres.
insights.so_what: Points to a growing market for self-hosted inference tooling and pressure on premium API margins.
insights.quote: This will get commoditized and you will run your own inference stacks soon enough.
insights.locator: As users, long context is powerful
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: For a modest 4-billion-parameter model (36 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 dimensions, FP8), each token occupies about 72 KB of KV cache, so a 20,000-token prompt consumes roughly 1.6 GB of GPU memory.
insights.so_what: Long-context agentic workloads are memory-bound, driving demand for GPU memory and cache tiers.
insights.quote: 72 kilobytes per token, a 20,000 token prompt is 1.6 gigabyte.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: GPU memory is small relative to KV cache needs: the tested cheaper GPU had 24 GB while expensive Blackwell parts have 192 GB, making per-user gigabytes of state expensive in multi-tenant fleets.
insights.so_what: HBM capacity per GPU is a binding constraint on inference concurrency and margins.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: KV cache entries are not reusable per token like a hashmap; each value depends on all preceding tokens, so cache reuse requires an exact prefix match and losing any block forces recomputation of everything after it.
insights.so_what: Prompt structure (stable prefixes) determines cache hit rates and therefore inference cost.
insights.quote: If you have lost and if you have evicted even like one link in the chain, you have to go recompute the whole thing.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: A trivial bug in Llama.cpp, injecting a timestamp before the prompt, invalidated the entire KV cache and forced full prefill each time; Shams's team committed a patch for it.
insights.so_what: Hidden prefix-breaking choices can silently multiply GPU cost.
insights.locator: In fact, one of my team members
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Claude Code achieves high cache hit rates because it appends each turn to the prior prompt rather than sending a new one, which is also why token consumption grows over a session until compaction.
insights.so_what: Agentic coding tools are architected around prefix caching, central to provider unit economics.
insights.locator: If you pay attention to your Claude Code
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Anthropic and OpenAI give roughly a 90% price discount on cache-hit tokens, but that figure is a convenient pricing number, not a reflection that cached tokens are ten times cheaper for the provider.
insights.so_what: Cache-hit pricing is a margin lever; customers designing for cache hits cut costs sharply.
insights.quote: I think they give you like a 90% discount if you have a cache hit rate. That doesn't mean that it's ten times cheaper for them.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Changing an MCP server's tool list resets the prompt prefix and breaks caching, though this may be deliberate to avoid distracting the model with stale tools.
insights.so_what: Agent protocol design choices carry hidden inference cost.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: In a simulated agentic coding workload (10,000-token system prompt, 12 turns growing to ~22,800 tokens) on a 4B model with vLLM on an AWS G6 instance, 12 concurrent sessions gave p50 time-to-first-token of 1 second and p99 of 2.6 seconds.
insights.so_what: Baseline for how few long-context sessions a cheap GPU can serve well.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Raising concurrency from 12 to 14 sessions pushed the KV cache past GPU memory and p99 time-to-first-token jumped from 2.6 seconds to 38.9 seconds, a swap-like cliff driven by eviction and recomputation.
insights.so_what: Inference performance is nonlinear in load; capacity planning errors are catastrophic for tail latency.
insights.quote: The p99 jumps from 2.6 seconds before at 12 concurrent to 38.9 seconds.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Adding 16 GB of host DRAM as a KV cache tier cut p99 at 14 sessions from 38.9 seconds to about 3.5 seconds, and 32 GB pushed the concurrency cliff from 14 to 28 sessions, while 8 GB barely helped.
insights.so_what: Cheap DRAM can roughly double effective GPU concurrency, supporting demand for server DRAM in inference boxes.
insights.quote: if you add 32 gigabytes of local DRAM, you can push your concurrency cliff from 14 to 28.
insights.locator: With that out of the way
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Even though DRAM is getting more expensive, it remains far cheaper than GPU VRAM and copying KV state from terabytes of DRAM is still cheaper than recomputing it.
insights.so_what: Structural demand for large DRAM pools attached to GPU servers.
insights.quote: You have terabytes of it and it's still going to be cheaper than recomputing it.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: NVMe SSDs offer tens of terabytes for KV cache but constant large KV writes can exhaust SSD write endurance quickly; each storage tier trades latency for capacity, with recomputation as the bottom tier.
insights.so_what: KV offload may accelerate SSD wear and replacement cycles in inference fleets.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: For a remote KV cache, time to first byte matters little; what matters is throughput and saturating the NIC, best achieved by chunking gigabyte contexts into many megabyte-sized objects fetched in parallel.
insights.so_what: Remote KV caching is a bandwidth business, favoring high-throughput networking and storage vendors.
insights.quote: Your goal when building something like this for a remote KV cache is to saturate the NIC.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: High-end GPU instances costing around $50 per hour have terabits per second of network bandwidth, versus 25 gigabit on the modest G6 instance.
insights.so_what: Networking capacity is integral to inference economics at scale.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Valkey, the Redis fork backed by Amazon and Google, added I/O threads so the single main thread no longer blocks while writing multi-megabyte objects to the NIC, which determines whether the full NIC can be used for KV caching.
insights.so_what: Open-source cache infrastructure is being repurposed for AI inference workloads.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Copy avoidance has been the most profound optimization on both server and client; writing an inference client in Rust with native bindings can slow things down because of extra copies across Rust, Python, CUDA, and GPU memory.
insights.so_what: Language rewrites are not a performance shortcut; data movement dominates.
insights.quote: This is a classic example of when Rust will slow you down.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Admission control by concurrency count fails in multi-tenant inference because a single 100,000-200,000-token prompt can thrash everyone out of VRAM; operators must admit based on per-token KV cost, KV budget, and a cliff estimate.
insights.so_what: Workload mix, e.g. a new Claude Code release, can upend inference fleet capacity planning.
insights.quote: You really can't make any assumptions on being able to admit by concurrency count.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Naive sticky sessions to GPUs create bank-run-like hotspots under spiky agentic workloads, and fleet-wide p99 latency follows the hottest node.
insights.so_what: Load-balancing intelligence is a differentiator for inference platforms.
insights.quote: Your fleet-wide p99 is going to follow your hottest node.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: In Shams's test, naively scaling from one GPU (110 tokens/s) to two yielded only 128 tokens/s (58% efficiency), while session-aware routing reached 201 tokens/s; three and four GPUs reached 278 and 324 tokens/s.
insights.so_what: KV-aware routing nearly doubles throughput on the same hardware.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Mooncake uses proactive KV migration to pre-empt hotspots, and NVIDIA's Dynamo routes requests to the node holding the longest prefix while balancing against hotspots.
insights.so_what: NVIDIA is extending its moat into inference orchestration software.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Disaggregating prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bandwidth-bound) onto separate nodes lets each scale independently and prevents long prefills from slowing other decodes, and specialized decode-optimized hardware is now being built.
insights.so_what: Opens room for specialized decode accelerators alongside GPUs.
insights.quote: there are specific hardware that are now being built that are optimized primarily for the decode stage
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Cache-aware remote placement, prefill/decode disaggregation, and mobile KV state were controversial six months earlier but the industry is now converging on them.
insights.so_what: Signals a settled architecture for inference that vendors will standardize around.
insights.quote: These things about six months ago were still super controversial, but now it seems like everybody is converging
insights.locator: Like if you don't say it runs locally
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Recomputation-heavy prefill under cache thrashing can also cause GPUs to run hot and hit thermal throttling, compounding latency.
insights.so_what: Poor cache management raises both compute and power/thermal costs.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Every token a user sends becomes state the provider must carry; Shams jokes that polite 'please' tokens erode Anthropic's margins, citing it as a $965 billion rather than trillion-dollar company.
insights.so_what: Token state is a real cost driver in provider margins.
insights.quote: The fact that you're saying please probably is why they couldn't become a trillion-dollar company, were only 965.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams

insights.claim: Running side tasks as sub-agents or separate sessions avoids diluting the prefix cache, improving output quality and reducing compaction frequency.
insights.so_what: Agent design around context locality lowers cost and improves quality.
insights.speaker: Khawaja Shams
